title: 1.e4 — Beginner
blurb: Classic king-pawn openings with simple, safe replies to every Black defence. The friendliest place to start.

lines.name: Italian Game (Giuoco Piano)
lines.plan: Slow build-up: keep the centre with c3/d3, reroute the b1-knight via d2–f1 to g3, then choose your break — d4 in the centre or kingside play with Nf5/Ng5 ideas. Never hurry; improve a piece each move.

notes.4: The Italian bishop — it points straight at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp (only the king defends it).
notes.6: Prepares d4: after c3, the d4 push comes with pawn support and Black's bishop must give ground.
notes.8: The modern, patient choice. The centre is solid; the fight moves to slow manoeuvring, which is easier to play.
notes.10: Castle early in open games — e-file tactics punish a king left in the middle.
notes.12: The rook supports e4 and quietly waits behind a future d4 break.
notes.14: Mirrors Black's queenside grab: stops ...b5 gaining space and gives the c4-bishop an escape on a2.
notes.16: A little luft that also takes g4 from Black's pieces — no ...Bg4 pin, no ...Ng4 tricks.

lines.name: Italian vs ...Nf6 (Two Knights, quiet)
lines.plan: You reach the same Giuoco Pianissimo structure: c3/d3, Re1, a4, then the d4 break or the Nbd2–f1–g3 knight tour. The move order differs; the plan does not.

notes.5: Black develops with a threat against e4 — the Two Knights Defence.
notes.6: Simply defend e4. The sharp 4.Ng5 exists, but d3 keeps you in familiar Italian territory with zero risk.
notes.10: Standard furniture: rook behind the e-pawn before any central break.
notes.12: Space on the queenside and a retreat square (a2) for the bishop.
notes.14: The usual tandem with d3 — one day you play d4 in one go, fully supported.
notes.16: The dream tour begins: this knight is heading d2–f1–g3 (or c4), the signature Italian manoeuvre.

lines.name: Italian move order: 3...Nf6 4.d3 Bc5
lines.plan: If Black plays ...Nf6 before ...Bc5 you simply transpose: same pawn skeleton (c3+d3), same rook on e1, same knight tour. One setup, whatever the order.

notes.7: Black returns to Giuoco lines — you're back in the main plan, just via a different door.
notes.10: Same idea as always: prop up a future d4.
notes.16: The finishing touch of the setup — g4 is off-limits and the back rank breathes.

lines.name: vs Sicilian — Alapin (2...d5)
lines.plan: You get an isolated-queen-pawn-style centre with easy development. Keep pieces active, watch the d4 pawn, and use the open lines — trades favour Black, activity favours you.

notes.2: The Alapin: sidestep the huge Open Sicilian theory and just build a big centre with d4.
notes.4: Trade before Black gets ...d4 in — the queen recapture exposes Her Majesty to your tempo-gaining moves.
notes.6: The point of c3: a full pawn centre while Black's queen sits in the open.
notes.10: Calmly break the pin. No weaknesses, and O-O comes next.
notes.14: Reinforce d4 before Black piles up on it — the whole game revolves around that pawn.
notes.16: Recapture toward the centre. You may end up with an isolated d-pawn: that's fine, it buys open lines and outposts.

lines.name: vs Sicilian — Alapin (2...Nf6)
lines.plan: Black's knight gets kicked around while you build the centre. Develop with tempo (Bc4 hits the knight's squares), keep d4 healthy, and enjoy a risk-free space edge.

notes.3: The critical reply — attacking e4 before you play d4.
notes.4: Push with tempo. The knight must move again; you win time for the centre.
notes.8: The centre arrives on schedule, protected by c3.
notes.12: Develop with a question: the d5-knight is now uncomfortable.
notes.14: Keep the bishop and pin the c6-knight — e5 is suddenly hard to win back.
notes.16: Recapture with the knight and keep the pressure: the pin on c6 means Black must untangle carefully.

lines.name: vs Sicilian — Alapin (2...e6)
lines.plan: A French-like structure where you often win the c5-pawn tension. Play against the isolated d5-pawn: blockade it with a knight on d4, trade dark-square defenders, and press.

notes.4: Take the full centre — Black's ...e6 means no early piece pressure against it.
notes.6: Clarify: Black gets an isolated d-pawn to babysit for the rest of the game.
notes.10: A useful check: whatever blocks it becomes slightly misplaced.
notes.14: Win the tension at the right moment — the recapture costs Black another tempo.
notes.16: Heading for b3 or f1–g3: knights love the light squares around Black's isolated pawn.

lines.name: vs French — Exchange
lines.plan: A symmetric structure where the better developer wins. Post the bishop pair actively (Bd3+Bg5), put knights on e5/g3, and build a kingside attack while Black mirrors you a tempo behind.

notes.4: The Exchange: no French pawn chains, no theory debates — just a clean, open game where White moves first.
notes.8: The bishop's best diagonal — it stares at h7 for the whole middlegame.
notes.12: A real pin: Black's f6-knight holds the kingside together.
notes.14: Flexible: the knight can go f1–g3 or c4–e5. Symmetry is only equal if Black finds every good square too.
notes.16: A modest move with a purpose: b4-b5 space later, and the d4-pawn never worries again.

lines.name: vs Caro-Kann — Exchange
lines.plan: The classic "carlsbad" attack: Qb3 pokes at b7, knights come to e5/f3, and the minority ideas (b4-b5) or a kingside build-up follow. Simple squares, clear plan.

notes.4: Trade into a structure YOU know better: this is a Queen's Gambit Exchange with colours reversed and an extra tempo.
notes.6: Grab the b1-h7 diagonal before Black's bishop can contest it with ...Bf5.
notes.8: Solidify d4 and open c2 for the queen.
notes.10: The bishop takes the best diagonal outside the pawn chain before ...Bg4/...e6 locks things.
notes.12: Double attack: b7 hangs and d5 feels pressure. Black must contort to cover both.
notes.14: Note the move order: this knight develops first so f3 stays free for the g1-knight, keeping ...Bxf3 harmless.
notes.16: Everything is connected: next comes O-O, Rfe1 or the thematic Ne5.

lines.name: vs Scandinavian
lines.plan: You lead development by two tempi. Castle long, launch the kingside pawns or break with d5/Ne5 — the classic Scandinavian squeeze. Watch for ...Bxf3 and ...Qxd4 tricks; Bd2 and Qe2 cover them.

notes.2: Accept — the whole point of the Scandinavian is that Black recaptures with the queen and you develop with tempo.
notes.4: Develop AND hit the queen. Free moves like this are why 1...d5 is rare at the top.
notes.12: A quiet star move: it covers the c3-knight (so ...Qxc3 tricks vanish) and eyes the a5-queen along the diagonal.
notes.14: Connect the rooks and prepare O-O-O — the rook lands on d1 glaring at Black's queen file.
notes.16: Castle INTO the attack: your king is safe behind a-b-c pawns while every white piece points at Black's position.

lines.name: vs Pirc / Modern — Classical
lines.plan: Meet the fianchetto calmly: full centre, natural development, castle short. When ...e5 comes, keep the tension or trade favourably; your extra space means every trade eases your game, not theirs.

notes.6: The Classical setup: no sharp pawn storms to memorise, just good squares and a space edge.
notes.8: Modest but ideal: it lets you castle and later supports g4 or f3 if the game sharpens.
notes.12: Clip Black's queenside expansion before it starts — ...b5 was the Pirc's main source of play.
notes.15: Black finally stakes a claim in the centre — the thematic Pirc break.
notes.16: Keep everything: g4 is denied to Black's pieces, and you can choose between dxe5, d5, or simply Be3 next.

lines.name: vs Philidor (2...d6)
lines.plan: Open the centre and enjoy more space and freer pieces. Regroup with Re1/Bf1 (a Ruy Lopez trick), expand with a4/b4 or f4 later — Black is solid but passive; patience wins.

notes.3: The Philidor: solid, but it blocks the f8-bishop — Black accepts a cramped game.
notes.4: Strike immediately; if Black holds the centre with ...Nd7 lines you keep space, if ...exd4 the position opens for your better pieces.
notes.14: Rooks belong on the (half-)open file — and it discourages any ...d5 break tricks.
notes.16: The same regrouping Black just did: the bishop redeploys, the rook keeps the file, and g3/Bg2 or b3/Bb2 comes next.

lines.name: vs Petroff (2...Nf6)
lines.plan: A symmetric-ish middlegame where your c4/Nc3 pressure on d5 gives a lasting initiative. Keep pieces on, target the e4-knight's retreat squares, and expand with c4-c5 or central trades at the right time.

notes.3: The Petroff: instead of defending e5, Black counterattacks e4.
notes.4: Take first. The famous trap: if Black grabs 3...Nxe4? immediately, 4.Qe2! wins material — the knight is pinned to a discovered check.
notes.8: Claim the centre while the e4-knight decides where it lives.
notes.14: The main strike: hit d5 so the e4-knight loses its anchor.
notes.16: Sidestep and keep the tension — the b4-knight will have to come back, and cxd5 hangs over Black.

title: 1.d4 — London System
blurb: One setup against almost everything: Bf4, e3, Nf3, Bd3, c3. Low theory, very sturdy.

lines.name: London vs ...d5 (classical)
lines.plan: The full London dream: knight to e5, f-pawn or queen joins, and the pieces mass at Black's king. If Black trades on e5, recapture toward the kingside and attack down the f-file or with h4-h5.

notes.2: The London move: the bishop gets OUT before e3 closes the door. Everything else is the same wall: e3, Nf3, Bd3, c3, Nbd2.
notes.4: The wall goes up. Note the bishop is already outside it.
notes.7: Black offers the trade of your good bishop — never take; make Black decide.
notes.8: Tuck it back. If Black ever takes on g3, hxg3 opens the h-file straight at their king — a free attacking file.
notes.12: The second wall brick: d4 is now rock solid whatever Black throws at it.
notes.14: This knight covers e4/c4 and frees the other one for the star square...
notes.16: The London payoff: the knight lands on e5 for keeps. If ...Nxe5 dxe5, the pawn forks d6 and f6 and your pieces flood kingside.

lines.name: London vs ...c5
lines.plan: Identical setup, and the same Ne5 payoff. Against ...c5+...Qb6 poking, Qb1 or Qc1 holds b2 calmly — never let the b-pawn distract you from the kingside plan.

notes.3: Black strikes at d4 immediately — c3 will hold it forever.
notes.8: Now d4 is defended three times. The London doesn't fear ...cxd4 either: exd4 opens the e-file for you.
notes.10: Same routine, every game: this knight first, so Ne5 stays available for its partner.
notes.16: There it is again. Supported by d4 and f4-ideas, the knight cramps Black's whole position.

lines.name: London vs King's Indian setup
lines.plan: Against the fianchetto, stay compact: h3 keeps the bishop safe, c3 holds the centre. Meet ...e5 with dxe5 and use the d-file; meet ...Nh5 with Bh2, where the bishop keeps its diagonal. Play on the queenside with c4/b4 if the centre stays closed.

notes.3: A King's Indian setup — Black will aim ...e5 or ...d6/...Nbd7 at your centre.
notes.8: Quieter than Bd3 here: against a g6-bishop the light-squared bishop is a supporting actor, not the star.
notes.10: King first. The London never gets mated in the opening.
notes.12: A key little move: it gives the f4-bishop the h2 hideout, so ...Nh5 or ...e5-e4 never wins it.
notes.14: The usual glue. If ...e5 comes now: dxe5 dxe5, slide the bishop back and own the d-file.
notes.16: Setup complete. Next: a4 for space, or Qb1/Re1 depending on where Black commits.

lines.name: London vs ...e6 (Queen's-side setup)
lines.plan: Black delays ...d5 but usually plays it anyway — you transpose to the classical plan: Nbd2, Bd3, then Ne5 with a kingside build-up. One system, many doors in.

notes.8: Always this brick before Bd3 — otherwise ...Nb4 harasses the bishop.
notes.10: Back in known territory: it's the classical London with an extra move played by each side.
notes.16: The move the whole system is built around — cement it with f4 or trade into a kingside pawn storm.

lines.name: London vs ...c6 + ...Bf5 (Slav-like)
lines.plan: When Black copies your bishop idea, trade it off and claim the centre: Qxd3 keeps everything tidy, then e4! turns your "boring" wall into a real pawn centre. You get the freer game out of the symmetry.

notes.7: Black develops the bishop outside the wall too — the copycat approach.
notes.8: Offer the trade: your e-file recapture options mean the symmetric position quietly favours you.
notes.10: The queen is perfectly placed: it supports the coming e4 break.
notes.12: Both knights point at e4 now.
notes.16: The break that wins the centre: exchange on e4 leaves you freer, ignoring it lets you push e5 with space.

lines.name: London vs ...Qb6 (the b2 poke)
lines.plan: Qc1 defuses the queen sortie completely; Black's queen usually ends up misplaced on b6. Then normal service: Bd3/Bg3, O-O, Nbd2-e5 and the standard kingside build.

notes.9: The most annoying London poke: the queen hits b2, which the bishop left behind.
notes.10: The calm answer — b2 is covered, no weaknesses made, and your queen was headed this way (toward h6) anyway.
notes.16: Slightly humbler than d3 (the queen watches c-file matters), but the plan is unchanged: O-O, Ne5, kingside play.

lines.name: London vs Modern (...d6 + ...g6)
lines.plan: Same anti-fianchetto recipe as against the King's Indian: h3, c3, patient centre. If Black grabs space with ...e5, trade on e5 and target d6 down the file. Queenside expansion with a4-a5 is your slow win.

notes.12: The bishop's bolt-hole on h2, as always against ...g6 setups.
notes.16: Done. From here: a4, Qb1 or Re1 — pick the wing where Black is weakest.

lines.name: London vs ...Bg4 (the pin)
lines.plan: Invite the exchange on f3 — the queen recapture is comfortable and you keep the bishop pair. Then the standard centre (Nd2, Bd3, O-O) with the long-term plan of e4 and a slow kingside push.

notes.7: The pin — the sharpest try against the London's quiet setup.
notes.8: Put the question immediately: retreat (loses time) or trade (gives you the bishops).
notes.10: Perfectly safe: the queen even eyes b7 and supports a later e4.
notes.12: Toward e4-support duty. Black gave up a bishop for a knight, so you own the pair — keep the position rich and avoid further trades.
notes.16: Tuck the king away, then prepare e4 (Rfe1, Qe2 ideas) — the bishops want open lines.

lines.name: London vs early ...cxd4 (open centre)
lines.plan: With the c-file half open, park the queen's rook on c1 later and play against Black's queenside. The h3 question to the g4-bishop and a timely Ne5 remain your standard tools.

notes.5: Black releases the tension early — recapture toward the centre.
notes.6: Now the e-file is half open for your rook, and the bishop outside the chain is exactly where it wants to be.
notes.14: With c-tension resolved the queen finds work: b7 is sensitive and b-file play beckons.
notes.16: The standard question to the bishop — every retreat or trade improves your position slightly.

lines.name: London vs ...Be7 (flexible QGD style)
lines.plan: Against the modest ...Be7, take the e5 outpost early and build behind it: f4 if allowed, Qf3/Rf3 lifts in dream scenarios, or simply a solid plus with more space. The London plays itself here.

notes.7: Black declines the ...Bd6 trade offer — one less problem for your dark-squared bishop.
notes.16: Unchallenged by a d6-bishop, the knight is even stronger here. f4 next makes it permanent.

title: 1.e4 — Attacking
blurb: Sharp, initiative-grabbing lines: gambits with 1.e4 e5 and pointed setups against the Sicilian, French and Caro.

lines.name: Evans Gambit (accepted)
lines.plan: You are a pawn down with a monster centre and every piece aimed at the king. Keep the initiative at all costs: open files, deny Black castling (Ba3!), and convert the attack before Black consolidates. In the Evans you attack — quiet moves hand the extra pawn a future.

notes.6: The Evans Gambit: a wing pawn buys two tempi and a giant centre. Fischer called it "a lesson in time".
notes.8: Hit the bishop and prepare d4 — the pawn comes back to build the centre Black just helped you make.
notes.10: The point: a full centre, open lines, and Black already two moves behind in development.
notes.12: King safety first, THEN the storm. The d4-pawn can wait — it's pinned to your initiative.
notes.14: Centre restored. Note Black's pieces: bishop offside on a5, knights passive — that's what the pawn bought.
notes.16: Open it up! Every open line favours the better-developed side, and that's you by miles.
notes.18: The killer: this bishop cuts the f8–a3 diagonal, so Black's king is stuck in the centre. Now bring rooks to e1/c1.

lines.name: Two Knights — 4.Ng5 (main, 5...Na5)
lines.plan: You won a clean pawn; Black got activity. Give back a tempo or two calmly (Be2, Nf3, d3), untangle, and reach a middlegame where the extra pawn simply counts. Greed now, technique later.

notes.6: The most testing move on move four in all of chess: f7 is attacked twice and Black has no clean defence.
notes.8: Take — every Black reply has a cost. The main line 5...Na5 gives up a pawn for activity.
notes.10: Keep the extra pawn honest: this check forces ...c6, loosening Black's structure further.
notes.12: Second pawn — you'll return one for a smooth game, but make Black prove the compensation.
notes.14: The cold-blooded retreat (stronger than d3 lines): keep the bishop, blunt ...Qc7/...Bd6 batteries.
notes.16: Retreat with a plan: when ...e4 pushes, Ne5! centralises — the knight is superb there. See the Black-side pack for what Black intends; here you simply stay a pawn up.

lines.name: Fried Liver Attack (5...Nxd5?!)
lines.plan: A piece for two pawns and a king hunt. Keep checking and developing with tempo — d4, Bf4, O-O-O ideas. Black's king on e6 must survive twenty moves of pressure; one slip and it's mate. Know the ideas, not just moves: target d5 and f7-squares, keep the queen close.

notes.9: The natural recapture is the famous mistake — now the sacrifice works.
notes.10: The Fried Liver: a whole knight to drag the king into the open. Unsound? Engines say barely — humans never survive it.
notes.12: The queen enters with check and hits d5 — Black's king must step UP the board to hold the knight.
notes.14: Pile on d5. Every developing move comes with a threat; that's what makes the attack self-sustaining.
notes.16: Centralise and keep both threats alive (d5, plus mating nets on f5). The king on e6 blocks Black's whole army.
notes.18: Quietly ask the b4-knight to leave — it was the only defender doing real work.
notes.20: Open the centre on the pinned-in king: Bf4/O-O-O next, every piece joins, and Black's extra knight watches from a6.

lines.name: Scotch Gambit (Møller-style)
lines.plan: The d5 push splits Black's position in two. Follow up with Re1 and Rxe4 regains material with an ongoing initiative — or Black returns the piece and you emerge with the better structure. Study the ideas behind d5: it's a fork of concepts, not just squares.

notes.4: Open the centre immediately — the gambit spirit: development over material.
notes.6: Offer the d-pawn (again): taking it costs Black two more tempi while you castle and attack f7.
notes.10: Centre re-established, bishop must decide, and the fun begins.
notes.13: Black grabs the pawn and dares you to prove it — the critical test.
notes.15: Consistency: Black removes the knight to keep the extra pawn.
notes.16: The famous shot: ignore the bishop, fork c6 and open every line. After ...Bf6, Re1 wins the piece back with interest.

lines.name: vs Sicilian — Grand Prix Attack
lines.plan: The classic f-file attack: Qe1–h4, f5 at the right moment, Bh6 to trade the defender, and a rook lift if needed. Black's queenside counterplay races you — keep your foot down; tempo matters more than material on opposite wings.

notes.2: The smart move order: it dodges 2.f4 d5!, and f4 comes next anyway.
notes.4: The Grand Prix: you announce the plan on move three — pawn to f5, pieces to the king.
notes.8: Aim at f7 while it's soft; against ...e6 setups the bishop drops back to b3 keeping the diagonal.
notes.12: Modest centre on purpose: the pawns' job is to free the pieces for the kingside, not to win the middle.
notes.14: The signature lift: the queen swings to h4, where mating ideas with f5/Bh6/Ng5 appear naturally.
notes.16: Keep the bishop alive and the tension high — exd5 only when it opens lines toward the king.

lines.name: vs Sicilian — Open, English Attack
lines.plan: Opposite-side castling means a pure race: g4-g5 tears open the kingside while Black pushes ...b5. Speed rules — every non-attacking move is a wasted one. Trade off Black's defenders, never your attackers.

notes.4: The Open Sicilian: the most principled and most feared answer — take the centre and out-develop.
notes.10: The English Attack setup: Be3+f3+Qd2+O-O-O, one recipe against the whole Najdorf.
notes.14: The backbone: it guards e4, supports g4, and gives your king shelter after long castling.
notes.16: Queen and bishop battery — Bh6 ideas later, and O-O-O is ready.
notes.18: Kings on opposite wings: now it's a knife fight, and your g/h pawns are the knives.
notes.20: The storm begins. g5 evicts the f6-knight (the king's best defender), then h4-h5 rips the cover.

lines.name: vs French — Advance
lines.plan: Space is the point: e5 cramps Black forever. Hold d4 (the eternal French target), then expand kingside — Bd3, O-O, and the f4-f5 or Nf3-g5 ideas. If the queenside gets tense, b4-b5 gains even more room.

notes.4: The Advance: claim space, lock the centre, and leave Black's c8-bishop buried behind its own pawns.
notes.10: The modern main move: it prepares b4, grabbing queenside space and blunting Black's entire ...c5 pressure scheme.
notes.12: Expand with tempo — the c5-pawn must resolve, and your queenside becomes a second front.
notes.16: The bishop defends d4 from ambush. Black's pieces hit d4 three times; you hold it three times — the French stand-off, and you have the space.

lines.name: vs Caro-Kann — Panov Attack
lines.plan: Isolated queen's pawn chess at its best: use the d-pawn's cramp for piece activity — Bg5, Rc1/Re1, Ne5, and the classic d5 break or Bxh7 Greek-gift patterns. Trades drift toward equality, so keep the board full and the pieces pointed at the king.

notes.6: The Panov: the "boring" Caro suddenly becomes an open, initiative-driven IQP battle — on your terms.
notes.12: Resolve into the classic structure: your d4-passer-to-be versus Black's solid but passive setup.
notes.16: Everything natural: next Re1, a3/Bc2-Qd3 battery ideas, or Ne4 — the IQP attacking toolkit.

lines.name: Scotch Gambit — 4...Nf6 (declined)
lines.plan: A structure duel: your lead in development and pressure on c6/d4 versus Black's central knight. Play against the c6-pawns — Nd2 or Qe2 challenges the e4-knight, c4-ideas fix the weaknesses, and your pieces stay freer.

notes.7: Black declines the gambit and counterattacks — the sound, modern choice.
notes.8: Push with tempo; the knight must jump and the position opens exactly one line at a time — yours.
notes.10: Pin, protect the e5-pawn's advance guard duties, and keep the initiative flowing.
notes.12: Regain the pawn with a fine central knight. Material level, activity yours.
notes.14: Trade at the right moment: Black's pawns get doubled and c6 becomes a permanent target.
notes.16: Safety plus threat (f3 hitting e4 comes next). From here it's pressure against c6 and the better minor pieces.

title: vs 1.e4 — Caro-Kann
blurb: A rock-solid answer to 1.e4: a good pawn structure and an easy bishop, with little to memorise.

lines.name: Advance — Short system (...c5 break)
lines.plan: Your play is on the queenside and against d4: pile up with ...Nc6, ...Qb6, ...Rc8 on the half-open c-file. The e5-pawn cramps you slightly, but your bishop escaped BEFORE ...e6 — the whole point of the Caro over the French.

notes.5: The Caro-Kann promise kept: the bishop gets out before ...e6 walls it in. Compare the poor French bishop on c8.
notes.9: The thematic strike: hit d4 while White is mid-development. The c6-pawn's whole career was preparing this.
notes.11: Trade at your moment — the recapturing knight can be questioned later with ...Bc5 or ...Nc6.
notes.13: Flexible development: this knight can go c6 or g6, and ...Nd7 will follow. Slow is fine; the position is closed.
notes.15: Challenge the strong d4-knight immediately — trades ease your slightly cramped game.

lines.name: Exchange Variation
lines.plan: A reversed Queen's Gambit structure where you know the plans: complete development smoothly, then choose ...Rc8 with c-file pressure or the ...e5 break once pieces are placed. White's "attack" here is mostly a rumour — equalise, then outplay.

notes.4: The Exchange — White avoids theory, but hands you free, natural development.
notes.7: Develop with pressure on d4 before White gets c3 in comfortably... White usually does anyway; the tempo still helps you.
notes.9: Natural squares, no weaknesses — the Caro-Kann recipe.
notes.11: Your "problem piece" finds a job: it provokes weaknesses or trades itself for the f3-knight-to-be.
notes.13: Calmly hold b7. Note ...Na5 hitting the queen is also a resource here if White presses.
notes.15: Structure complete. Next ...Bd6 or ...Be7, castle, and the game is fully equal with play left in it.

lines.name: Classical (4...Bf5 main line)
lines.plan: The famous "boring but beautiful" Caro: your structure has no weaknesses, the h4-h5 pawns White threw forward may become targets, and endgames favour you. Castle queenside or short depending on White's setup; break with ...c5 when developed.

notes.5: Trade in the centre — the Classical: you accept less space for a position with zero weaknesses.
notes.7: Again the bishop escapes first. White's best try is chasing it — which costs time and loosens pawns.
notes.9: The bishop ducks; let White "win" tempi by weakening squares.
notes.11: Give the bishop an h7 hideout and take g5 from White's pieces. The h4-pawn may regret marching later.
notes.15: Tucked away safely. It looks passive; it will re-emerge after ...e6 and trades — the classic Caro bishop story.
notes.17: Trade into total safety: White's attacking bishop leaves the board.
notes.19: The wall completes. Next: ...Ngf6, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, castle, and equal chess with the healthier structure.

lines.name: vs Two Knights (2.Nf3 3.Nc3)
lines.plan: The trade on f3 solves all development questions. Aim for the reliable structure: ...e6, ...Nd7/...Ngf6, trade a pair of knights, and play the long game — your pawn formation has no targets.

notes.5: Against the Two Knights the pin is the right development: 3...dxe4 4.Nxe4 leaves the f5-bishop plans less smooth.
notes.7: Concede the bishop pair for rock-solid structure and easy equality — a very Caro trade.
notes.11: Take now that d4 was played: White's knight recaptures into your prepared piece trades.
notes.15: Develop and offer the trade — each exchange leaves White's bishop-pair "advantage" thinner.
notes.17: Recapture with the knight, keeping pawns tidy. Equal and easy to play: ...Bd6/...Be7 and castle next.

lines.name: vs Panov Attack
lines.plan: Blockade the isolated pawn: a knight parks on d5, pieces trade, and every exchange magnifies the weak pawn. Endgames are your friend — steer there and pick the d4-pawn up in round two.

notes.6: The Panov: White wants IQP activity. Your counter-plan is simple — blockade, trade, endgame.
notes.9: Solid: hold d5 firmly. The c8-bishop grumbles, but the blockade matters more here.
notes.13: The blockading knight arrives. From d5 it cannot be evicted by pawns — the IQP's permanent problem.
notes.17: Development done. Now ...Bf6/...Nce7 regroupings, pressure on d4, and patient simplification.

lines.name: vs Fantasy (3.f3)
lines.plan: Meet the eccentric with the classical: ...e5! strikes back immediately. The g4-pin is your key resource — the f3-knight is tied to the queen, so central tension favours you. Develop quickly; White's f3 took a square from the king's knight for a reason you exploit.

notes.4: The Fantasy Variation: White props up e4 oddly. Punish oddity with the centre strike.
notes.7: The counter-blow: with f3 gone, White's king diagonal is airy and d4 is under real pressure.
notes.9: The pin is the point: now dxe5?? drops the queen to ...Bxf3 tricks — check it: the knight is pinned to d1.
notes.11: Guard e5 and complete the idea — White's centre is frozen while you finish development.
notes.13: Everything defended, everything developed. White's early f3 bought nothing.
notes.15: Solid and active — castle next, keep the e5-strongpoint, and play against the loosened white king.

lines.name: vs King's Indian Attack (2.d3)
lines.plan: With White declining the centre, take it yourself: ...e5 and ...d5 give you the space for once. Keep the e5/d5 duo healthy, develop behind it, and meet White's slow kingside ideas with a faster queenside march (...b5-b4).

notes.2: The KIA: White plays a system, not against your moves. Fine — your system is bigger.
notes.5: The luxury the Caro rarely gets: a full pawn centre of your own. Take it.
notes.11: Castle behind your space advantage. White's usual KIA attack is far slower with c6+d5 blunting the g2-bishop.
notes.13: Overprotect e5 — the strongpoint the whole setup leans on.
notes.15: Complete and comfortable. Next ideas: ...b5, ...a5-a4 queenside space, or ...Bf8 regrouping if White pokes at e5.

lines.name: vs Advance, 4.Nc3 (Shirov's g4 lunge)
lines.plan: Don't fear the pawn storm — it loosens White more than you. Keep the bishop safe on g6, strike with ...c5 at the fixed d4-pawn, and remember: White's king also lives on that side of the board. Calm development beats wild pawns.

notes.6: The aggressive setup: White intends g4 and a kingside pawn avalanche.
notes.8: There it comes. Pawns can't checkmate — hold steady.
notes.10: Heading for f4 to bother your bishop — expected, and answerable.
notes.11: The counter-rule: a wing attack is met by a central strike. d4 creaks immediately.
notes.13: One prophylactic move: g5 is stopped, h5 can be met by ...Bh7, and White must now justify the loose pawns.

lines.name: vs 3.Nd2 (same as Classical)
lines.plan: Identical play to the Classical main line — White's knight took a different road to e4, nothing changes. Same trades, same wall, same healthy structure and long-game confidence.

notes.4: Just a different door into the Classical: after your next move it transposes exactly.
notes.17: The familiar trade — by now this position should feel like home.
notes.19: And the familiar wall. One repertoire, several White move orders — that's Caro-Kann efficiency.

lines.name: vs Accelerated Panov (2.c4)
lines.plan: Same song as the Panov: blockade on d5, trade pieces, target the d4-pawn. The early c4 even skips White's most dangerous setups — develop naturally and equalise without drama.

notes.2: The accelerated version — answer in the centre exactly as always.
notes.7: Recapture with the KNIGHT (not the queen): it lands on d5 as a permanent blockader.
notes.13: The standard shell. White has the IQP; you have the d5-square and the plan.
notes.15: Develop, castle, then ...Bf6 and ...Nce7-f5 pile on d4 — Panov positions, Caro solutions.

title: vs 1.e4 — Open Games (1...e5)
blurb: Meet 1.e4 head-on with 1...e5 — sound, principled replies to the Ruy Lopez, Italian, Scotch and the gambits.

lines.name: Ruy Lopez — Closed (Chigorin setup)
lines.plan: The eternal Spanish battle: your queenside space (...b5, ...c5, ...Na5-c4 ideas) versus White's central and kingside play. Keep the e5-strongpoint alive, meet d4 with exchanges only when your pieces are ready, and never touch your kingside pawns without reason.

notes.5: The Morphy move: put the question to the bishop before doing anything else. Almost universal, for good reason.
notes.7: Develop and hit e4 — White must attend to it (O-O and Re1 do, tactically: know that ...Nxe4 lines exist but need care).
notes.9: The Closed Ruy: sound, flexible, and playable for a lifetime. Sharp ...Nxe4 (Open) is a different world.
notes.11: Now this comes with tempo — the bishop drops back and your queenside expansion has begun.
notes.13: Cement e5. The centre holds; the plans can breathe.
notes.15: King safe. White's c3 telegraphs d4 — you're braced for it.
notes.17: The Chigorin manoeuvre: harass the Spanish bishop and stake out c4/b3 squares.
notes.19: Full queenside deployment — ...Qc7 and ...Nc6 return next, with a completely healthy game.

lines.name: Italian — Giuoco Pianissimo
lines.plan: Mirror White's slow build and you're simply equal: ...a6/...Ba7 keeps the bishop, ...h6 guards g5, and the ...Ne7-g6 or ...Be6 regroupings follow. The first player to lash out usually stands worse — let it be White.

notes.5: Symmetric and best: the bishop takes its ideal diagonal before ...Nf6 invites Ng5 complications.
notes.7: Hit e4 so White must spend a move on it — d3 keeps things quiet.
notes.13: Housekeeping with a point: it prepares ...Ba7, keeping the bishop's strong diagonal even if d4 ever comes with tempo.
notes.15: Tucked in and permanent: from a7 it eyes f2 for the whole game — a slow-burn asset.

lines.name: Two Knights — vs 4.Ng5 (the real test)
lines.plan: You gave a pawn for a lead in development and a bind: ...e4 and ...Bd6 chase White's pieces home. Keep the initiative — open the e-file, castle fast, and make the extra tempo count before White untangles. This is the fighting answer to the Italian.

notes.5: The Two Knights: inviting 4.Ng5 because you have a good answer prepared.
notes.7: Forced but excellent: block the f7-attack and open your game.
notes.9: THE move to remember: 5...Nxd5?? walks into the Fried Liver sacrifice. The knight hits the c4-bishop instead.
notes.14: White's best retreat; the pawn-grab is done and now you collect interest...
notes.15: Kick the intruder with gain of time — it has one safe road home.
notes.17: Advance with tempo again: the knight moves a fourth time while your pieces flow out.
notes.19: Challenge the proud knight immediately. You're a pawn down with monster activity — historically Black scores beautifully here.

lines.name: Scotch Game
lines.plan: The doubled c-pawns buy you the centre: ...d5 frees everything and your pieces reach natural, active squares. Play against White's e4/d3 structure, use the half-open b-file, and enjoy a full share of the middlegame.

notes.5: Don't cling to e5 — take and develop; the Scotch gives Black free piece play.
notes.9: Pin and pressure: e4 needs constant attention now.
notes.11: Toward the centre, opening the b-file — the doubled pawns control d5 and are hard to ever attack.
notes.13: The equalising break, right on schedule. Everything Black owns comes alive.
notes.17: Symmetrical safety; your bishop pair and central pawn give a comfortable, rich game.

lines.name: vs King's Gambit (3...d5, the modern cure)
lines.plan: Return the pawn instantly for smooth development and the better structure — White's f4/f-file dreams never materialise. Castle quickly, keep the f4-pawn as a long-term hostage, and play the middlegame a small but stable step ahead.

notes.2: The King's Gambit — romantic, and objectively harmless if you stay calm.
notes.3: Take first, THEN give it back on your terms.
notes.5: The modern antidote: open the centre while White's king diagonal is airy. No memorising defence-of-f4 theory.
notes.11: Recapture with the knight: development over pawns, principle over greed.
notes.13: Guard the f4-trophy and aim at White's soft kingside — the gambit's weaknesses cut both ways.
notes.15: Fully developed with the healthier king. White is still explaining where the compensation went.

lines.name: vs Vienna (3.f4 d5!)
lines.plan: The central counter beats the wing pawn every time: your e4-knight is a rock, ...f5 reinforced it, and White's position carries the weaknesses. Develop around the knight, castle, and let White prove something.

notes.3: Natural development that keeps every good option — and sidesteps the Vienna's trickiest ideas.
notes.5: The key strike, same spirit as against the King's Gambit: meet f4 with the centre, never with fear.
notes.7: A superb knight lands with tempo-free permanence: taking it (Nxe4 dxe4) just helps your structure.
notes.11: Safety first; the e4-knight needs no babysitting yet.
notes.13: Reinforce the outpost and gain kingside space — en passant lets White trade, but your pieces recapture happily.
notes.15: The f-file half-opens toward White's king and your pieces hum. A model anti-Vienna picture.

lines.name: vs Bishop's Opening
lines.plan: The ...c6/...d5 counter takes the centre and blunts the c4-bishop's whole idea. After the trades you develop naturally with a tidy structure — equal chess where knowing the plan (minority ideas, e-file play) is worth more than the move list.

notes.2: The Bishop's Opening — often just an Italian in disguise, but with tricks if you drift.
notes.5: The precise reply: prepare ...d5 and ask the bishop what it's doing on c4.
notes.7: There it is: the full centre, with the bishop biting on granite.
notes.11: The practical block: trade the checking piece and simplify toward comfortable equality.
notes.13: The b8-knight recaptures, keeping f6's partner flexible and the d5-pawn covered.
notes.15: Actively placed, ready to castle — your centre pawn and easy game already shade the position your way.

lines.name: Ruy Lopez — Exchange (4.Bxc6)
lines.plan: You have the bishop pair forever; White has a healthier pawn majority. Keep pieces on (endgames with queens off favour White's structure), open lines for the bishops, and use ...c5/...Bg4 activity — the two bishops out-argue the doubled pawns in a middlegame.

notes.6: The Exchange: White bets on structure. You bet on the bishop pair — a good bet in the middlegame.
notes.8: Necessary care: 5.Nxe5? Qd4! forks knight and e4-pawn, regaining everything with interest. White knows this and castles.
notes.9: Solid protection of e5 — unusual-looking, standard, and strong: the e5-pawn holds the centre for the bishops.
notes.11: Trade on your terms.
notes.13: Gain a tempo and activate: the doubled pawn does honest work.
notes.15: Into the "endgame" without fear: with two bishops and active pieces, this queenless middlegame is fine for Black — theory's verdict, not bravado.
notes.17: The point: immediate activity. The rook is pushed around and your development completes with threats.

lines.name: vs Evans Gambit (decline it!)
lines.plan: Declining keeps all the positional pluses and none of the danger: White's b4/a4 pawns are loose in the long run. Develop normally, castle, hit the centre with ...d6/...Nf6 — the gambiteer gets no open lines and no fun.

notes.6: The Evans. Accepting is playable but memory-heavy — declining is the practical repertoire choice.
notes.7: One square back, all problems solved: the bishop keeps its diagonal and b4 hangs in some lines.
notes.13: The pawns overreached — trade and let White's queenside show its scars.
notes.15: Simple development with a hit on e4. White's "attack" turned into loose pawns and a normal game where you're fine.

lines.name: vs Four Knights (Spanish, Metger unwind)
lines.plan: The Metger manoeuvre untangles everything: ...Qe7 and ...Nd8-e6 re-route, ...Bxc3 removed the pressure, and the symmetric structure holds. A dependable, theory-light answer to White's most solid try.

notes.7: Mirror the pin — the classical equaliser in the Four Knights.
notes.13: The precise moment: remove the knight BEFORE Nd5 makes the g5-pin genuinely annoying.
notes.15: The Metger unwind begins: queen steps up so the d8-knight tour (d8–e6) can dissolve the pin.

lines.name: vs Centre Game (2.d4)
lines.plan: White's early queen is your target: develop with tempo, castle fast, and open the centre while the queen wanders. With opposite-side castling looming, your attack usually arrives first — ...Re8, ...d5 or even rook-takes-e4 tricks are in the air.

notes.2: The Centre Game: White wins the centre pawn but the queen must come out early to hold it.
notes.5: Develop with tempo — the queen moves again, you develop for free. The whole opening in one idea.
notes.9: Pin and pressure; White's setup only works if you let the e4/f2 tricks coordinate.
notes.13: The rook glares at e4 and the airy white queen — every central break now lands with double force.

title: vs 1.d4 — Slav / QGD
blurb: Classical, dependable answers to 1.d4 — hold the centre with ...d5 and develop naturally.

lines.name: Slav Defense (main line, 4...dxc4)
lines.plan: The Czech Slav promise: the c8-bishop develops OUTSIDE the pawn chain before ...e6. Play for ...c5 or ...e5 breaks once developed, keep the b4-bishop pressuring, and enjoy a position with no weak squares and real winning chances.

notes.3: The Slav: defend d5 with a pawn, keeping the c8-bishop's diagonal open — the improvement on the old QGD.
notes.7: The main line: win a tempo — White must spend a move (a4) to get the pawn back, and that move weakens b4.
notes.9: The point of everything: the bishop reaches its dream square before ...e6 closes the door.
notes.13: Onto the square a4 weakened — pinning and preparing smooth castling.
notes.17: The last piece finds its place; ...Bg6, ...Qa5 or the ...e5/...c5 breaks come next depending on White's setup.

lines.name: Slav — Exchange (drawish? only if you let it)
lines.plan: Symmetry is a truce, not a draw: keep the last pieces on, fight for the e4/e5 squares, and let White run out of ideas first. Your setup is bulletproof — winning attempts by White create the weaknesses you'll play against.

notes.4: The Exchange Slav — White hopes for a handshake. Decline politely.
notes.11: Symmetry maintained — and your bishop is just as good as White's.
notes.15: Trade on YOUR initiative: the queen recapture blocks White's d-file ambitions for a moment.
notes.18: White trades; recapture and the position is dead level with all the play still ahead.

lines.name: QGD — Tartakower (the lifetime system)
lines.plan: The Tartakower has served world champions for a century: ...b6 solves the bad bishop (it goes to b7), the ...c5 break equalises space, and the structure bends but never breaks. Learn its ideas once, play it forever.

notes.3: The Queen's Gambit Declined: the most classical answer in chess — hold d5 with the e-pawn.
notes.7: Break the pin calmly. The QGD is a fortress built one modest move at a time.
notes.11: A useful nudge: the bishop must declare itself, and h6 gives your king air forever.
notes.13: The Tartakower move: the "problem" c8-bishop gets the long diagonal, and ...c5 gains support.
notes.15: There it is — from b7 the bishop watches e4 and supports every central break.
notes.17: Happily recapture: the two bishops in a position about to open with ...c5 — a fair trade for White's "pressure".
notes.19: Keep the centre pawn: d5 controls e4/c4, and your pieces develop around it comfortably.

lines.name: QGD — Exchange (know the Carlsbad)
lines.plan: The Carlsbad structure: White plays for the minority attack (b4-b5); you counter in the centre or on the kingside — ...Ne4, the ...f5 clamp, or timely ...c5 breaks. Piece placement is everything: knights to d6? no — to e4 and g6-f4 dreams; rook to e8; bishop out before the wall closes.

notes.4: The Exchange QGD: White fixes the structure early, aiming for the famous minority attack.
notes.9: Standard unpinning; your structure decisions are already made, so develop with purpose.
notes.13: Toward f8/g6 or b6 — in the Carlsbad, knights choose careers early.
notes.15: Safe, and ready for the thematic ...Re8 and ...Ne4 — your standard counters to the queenside creep.
notes.17: The rook takes the file it will own all game. When b4-b5 comes, ...Ne4 and kingside play answer it.

lines.name: vs London System
lines.plan: Don't copy the London player's autopilot — question it: ...c5 pressure, ...b6/...Bb7, and a well-timed ...Ne4 or ...Bf5 trade. The London is comfortable only until Black takes the initiative on the queenside; that's your job here.

notes.2: The London — you'll see it constantly, so this line earns its keep.
notes.7: Ask the question immediately: trading on d6 helps you, retreating to g3 lets you ignore it.
notes.11: The break that gives Black real play — hit d4 while White's c3 hasn't arrived.
notes.15: The full plan: ...Bb7, ...Qe7 or ...Rc8, and pressure the queenside where London players drift.
notes.17: Develop calmly — the e5-knight looks proud but ...Nxe5 followed by central breaks defuses it whenever you choose.

lines.name: vs Catalan (open, ...dxc4 + ...b5)
lines.plan: You grabbed c4 and kept it long enough to develop ...Bb7 — the Catalan bishop bites on your b5/c6 pawns. Consolidate (...Nbd7, ...c5 later), return the pawn only for full equality, and neutralise the g2-diagonal with your own bishop.

notes.4: The Catalan: White's g2-bishop wants to own the long diagonal all game. Your plan: blunt it.
notes.11: The open Catalan: take the pawn at the moment White can't recapture cheaply.
notes.13: Hold the extra pawn a little longer — White must work (Qxc4 loses time to your next move).
notes.15: The tempo hit that makes the whole line: the queen retreats and your bishop claims the diagonal FIRST.
notes.17: Mission accomplished: the Catalan bishop stares at its reflection. ...Nbd7 and ...c5 finish the job.

lines.name: vs Colle / Torre setups
lines.plan: Against system players, seize the moment the system commits: your free c5/cxd4 tension and the e4-square are the prizes. After White's e4 push, trade into a position where you have the freer pieces and clear targets.

notes.4: The Colle: modest, popular at club level, and answerable with natural moves.
notes.7: Strike before the wall sets: the c-file tension is yours to manage all game.
notes.11: Mirror the good bishop diagonal — when White finally plays e4, you're the readier side.
notes.15: Recapture and re-aim: the bishop found an even better diagonal.
notes.19: One prudent retreat (the knight was eyeing c5) and the position is simply equal — with you knowing the plans: ...b6, ...Bb7, minor-piece trades.

lines.name: vs Torre Attack (3.Bg5)
lines.plan: The Torre wants a cheap grip on e5; deny it with ...c5 and ...h6 questions. Fianchetto the c8-bishop, trade off pressure, and reach a middlegame where White's "system" gave no edge and you have the clearer plan (minority-style queenside play or a central break).

notes.4: The Torre Attack — a pin with no knight on f6's partner square to back it up yet.
notes.7: Put the question early: every bishop decision helps you.
notes.9: Fix the centre while the bishop is offside.
notes.11: Unpin at leisure — White's d4-pawn is now the game's only static feature, and it's a target.
notes.15: The reliable setup: long diagonal, ...d6 or ...d5 to choose, and easy equality against the system.

lines.name: vs Trompowsky (2.Bg5)
lines.plan: Recapture with the e-pawn and embrace the doubled f-pawns: they control e5/g5, the half-open e-file suits your rooks, and the two bishops are long-term interest. Play ...Bd6, castle, then ...f5 or central breaks — the "damage" is your dynamism.

notes.2: The Trompowsky: White offers structure damage for the bishop pair — accept the trade on your terms.
notes.5: The right recapture: open e-file, e5 under control, and the f6-pawn guards kingside squares. Doubled ≠ weak.
notes.7: The bishop takes the b8–h2 diagonal the trade left unguarded.
notes.9: Take when it costs White a tempo to regain.
notes.13: Toward b6 or f8-g6: flexible, solid, and the bishops wait for the board to open.
notes.15: Gain the tempo back (the bishop must move) and clamp c4/d5 — full equality with the richer position.

lines.name: vs Slow Slav (4.e3 with ...Bf5)
lines.plan: When White plays quietly, your bishop STILL gets out first — that's the Slav's whole identity. If Nh4 chases it, the trade leaves you with the sounder structure and g6 as a useful lever. Then ...Nbd7, ...Be7-or-d6, castle, equal and easy.

notes.6: The quiet Slav — no a4 pin-downs, so develop the bishop immediately.
notes.10: White's only real try: hunt the bishop before the wall completes.
notes.11: Stand firm — capturing on g6 opens YOUR h-file and repairs nothing for White.
notes.15: Develop as normal: the half-open h-file is a small permanent gift, and your structure has no holes.
